extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, students of poetry, and educated readers interested in poetic evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging poets and poetic works (quality, arrangement, moral content, lasting reputation), drawn from Victorian literary criticism of Wordsworth and George Sand. Useful for critics, students, and editors assessing poetic greatness and editorial presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noble and profound application of ideas to life
rubrics_metrics.description: A great poet receives his distinctive character of superiority from his application ... to his subject of the ideas 'On man, on nature, and on human life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the poet powerfully applies broad ideas about man, nature, and human life under the conditions of poetic beauty and poetic truth; this application is the essential part of poetic greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as a criticism of life ('how to live')
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is at bottom a criticism of life; the greatness of a poet lies in his powerful and beautiful application of ideas to life,--to the question: How to live.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge poems by their engagement with moral/life questions rather than merely by ornament or technical skill; consider whether the work addresses human conduct, purpose, and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energetic and profound treatment of moral ideas (not mere didacticism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Voltaire's praise: 'no nation has treated in poetry moral ideas with more energy and depth than the English nation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between genuine poetic treatment of moral ideas (integrated, profound) and shallow didactic poetry; moral ideas should be applied under poetic truth and beauty, not reduced to sermonizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth versus abstract verbiage or systematic philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages of abstract philosophy (as in Wordsworth's Excursion) may carry us no step farther than the proposition they interpret and are 'a tissue of elevated but abstract verbiage, alien to the very nature of poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether philosophical material attains the character of poetic truth; philosophical doctrine in verse should be concrete, imaginatively embodied, and poetically true rather than merely abstract or systematized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality consistency within a poet's corpus (avoid mixed excellence and inferiority)
rubrics_metrics.description: In collections of short pieces the impression made by one piece requires to be continued and sustained by the piece following; Wordsworth's fine pieces are too often dulled by inferior pieces coming after them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the consistency of quality across a collection; a poet's reputation suffers when excellent works are embedded among markedly inferior ones—editors/critics should note the effect of juxtapositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate classification and arrangement of poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordsworth classified his poems according to a scheme of mental physiology; this is 'ingenious but far-fetched' and 'unsatisfactory.' The Greek categories (epic, dramatic, lyric) have a natural propriety and should be adhered to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poet's works are grouped according to natural poetic kinds (predominant strain determines category); poor or artificial arrangement can obscure a poet's strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial pruning: heavy output can hinder fame
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether or not the number of George Sand's works--always fresh, always attractive, but poured out too lavishly and rapidly--is likely to prove a hindrance to her fame ... Posterity always seeks to leave behind everything but masterpieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the quantity of a writer's output dilutes their best work; editors and posterity may need to 'clear away' inferior or excessive material to allow masterpieces to speak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shorter pieces often contain a poet's best work
rubrics_metrics.description: The best work is in his shorter pieces ... his poems of greatest bulk are by no means Wordsworth's best work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising a poet, give careful weight to shorter poems; large-scale poems should be judged separately and may not represent the poet's highest achievements.

rubrics_metrics.name: The poet's overall body of work matters more than isolated pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: It is, I say, by the great body of powerful and significant work which remains to him, after every reduction and deduction has been made, that Wordsworth's superiority is proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a poet by the cumulative power, interest, and enduring qualities of their oeuvre rather than solely by a few celebrated lines or single works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of poetry have relative status (hierarchy of poetic kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some kinds of poetry are in themselves lower kinds than others. The ballad kind is a lower kind; the didactic kind, still more, is a lower kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing poets, take into account the genre/kind of their poetry; value may vary by kind and some kinds contribute less to 'poetic greatness' in the critic's view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and formal finish are means, not ends ('inns' metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Style, form and argumentative ingenuity bear to life the relation which inns bear to home ... I attack the resting in them, the not looking to the end which is beyond them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether style, form, or technical cleverness serve deeper poetic ends; do not reward works that prioritize self-conscious style over substantive engagement with life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic solidity required for universal moral claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the 'intimations' ... have not the character of poetic truth of the best kind; to say universally that the instinct of delight in Nature is mighty in childhood and fades is 'to say what is extremely doubtful.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize broad psychological or moral claims in poetry for evidential and poetic solidity; universals asserted in verse should withstand doubt and be convincingly embodied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dealing with life as a whole confers superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Wordsworth's superiority: he deals with more of life than they do; he deals with life as a whole, more powerfully.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the scope of a poet's concern: poets who encompass a wide, comprehensive view of human experience are ranked higher for breadth and power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by impartial, international judgment (posterity/Amphictyonic Court)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be recognized by the verdict of such a confederation ... is indeed glory ... a tribunal free from national and provincial partiality putting a stamp on the best things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both national reputation and wider European/international recognition as measures of durable greatness; ephemeral popular vogue is less decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation management: remove 'poetical baggage' to aid recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: To be recognized far and wide as a great poet ... Wordsworth needs to be relieved of a great deal of the poetical baggage which now encumbers him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and editors may legitimately advocate selective publication/anthologizing to present a clearer view of a poet's best work and aid fair recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware critics who praise poets for the wrong reasons (e.g., formal philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Wordsworthians are apt to praise him for the wrong things, and to lay far too much stress upon what they call his philosophy. His poetry is the reality, his philosophy ... is the illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating praise, distinguish between valid poetic merits and attributes (like systematic philosophy) that may be secondary or misleading; prioritize poetic reality over doctrinal systematization.
